name: Hair tape-in / clip-in extensions

card.summary: Add-on hair wefts that attach by adhesive tape or clips for instant volume and length; the main documented risk is tension and adhesive damage to natural hair.
card.note: Prolonged tension or adhesive use is linked to traction alopecia and dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Tape-in and clip-in extensions are strands or wefts of human or synthetic hair that are attached to a person's own hair to add length or thickness. Clip-ins are fastened and removed by the wearer with small clips, while tape-ins are bonded to the natural hair with adhesive strips.

In appearance communities they are discussed as a way to add visible volume without a procedure, mostly by people with thin or short hair. No clinical trials were found that test their appearance benefit.
quick.mechanism: Hair wefts are attached to the natural hair (not the scalp) by clips or adhesive tape, adding visible density and length. They do not affect the underlying hair or follicles.
quick.risks: Dermatology references describe traction alopecia (hair loss at the hairline or around the ears) from prolonged tension, and adhesives can cause dermatitis or headaches. Wikipedia notes patch testing is advised before using bonding products.

lead: Hair extensions, also called weaves or hair integrations, add length or volume to natural hair by clipping, gluing or sewing in human or synthetic hair.[1] Tape-in and clip-in are two of the attachment methods listed for them, alongside micro or nano rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.[1]

In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions, extensions are mentioned as a non-surgical way to add apparent hair density. No clinical studies were found that evaluate extensions for appearance, and most published description concerns hair-care and hair-loss risks rather than aesthetic outcomes.[1]

paras: Extensions come as wefts or single strands made from human hair or synthetic fibers.[1] Human hair is described as the more expensive and more durable option, while synthetic fibers such as Kanekalon are cheaper but less durable and can look stiffer.[1] Most human hair used in the trade is reported to come from India, China and Vietnam.[1]

Methods of integration listed include track-and-sew, bonding glue, invisible-part techniques, thread sewing, tape-in and clip-in or clip-on.[1] The same source describes glue-based wefts as attached to natural hair rather than the scalp, and some methods as lasting around eight weeks.[1]
Wigs of many styles were fashionable by the late 17th century, and hair weaves emerged in the 1950s, initially among celebrities before becoming widespread in the 1970s.[1]

Prolonged wear can cause hair loss at the front hairline or above the ears, known as traction alopecia, and tight attachment can cause breakage and, in some cases, permanent follicle damage.[1] Glue is reported to cause headaches, bald spots and dermatitis; patch testing before using bonding products is advised.[1] These points come from a general encyclopedia article that carries a note about limited sourcing.
